L-classify-problems-int-spec-proy.statement: Problems are split into three kinds marked so they don't mix: interpreter, specification and project.

L-closed-observer.statement: Luthier is a closed, internally complete universe that observes the outside through a read/write boundary which is also a compilation.

L-closed-vs-open-definition.statement: A type can be defined closed, its carrier with operations and invariants together, or open, a bare carrier plus separately declared operations and laws that a model satisfies.

L-code-el-induction-recursion.statement: Code and El are defined mutually (induction-recursion), which in Luthier's vocabulary is a cycle, i.e. an object.

L-code-enables-autodiff.statement: Code that represents the calculations can be autodifferentiated and yield a step-by-step written result.

L-code-fixpoint-constructors.statement: Recursive types are described with var and mu constructors as a fixpoint, with strict positivity holding for free because Code has no arrow with var on the left.

L-code-is-data.statement: Code is data, erasing the distinction between code and data, following the Lisp model.

L-code-many-operations.statement: Luthier code is not merely compiled and run; many operations apply to it (verify, compile, run), giving more complexity but more expressivity.

L-code-obeys-laws-not-floats.statement: Floating-point numbers do not obey the algebraic laws of numbers, but the code is assumed to, so it can be reorganized for efficiency.

L-code-operations.statement: The language builds in functions that operate on code: tests, errors, derivatives, finding equivalents, and timing.

L-code-to-understand.statement: He codes to understand, which means being able to manipulate the code and see how changes affect its observables.

L-code-universe.statement: A data Code describes the type shapes that can be generated, El decodes each to a type, and the functors become ordinary Luthier functions over codes.

L-code-universe-requirements.statement: The code universe asks of Luthier mutual definition of Code and El, large elimination, and dependent pattern matching, so R11 is its prerequisite.

L-code-universe-staged.statement: Implement the code universe in stages: first codes without mu (numbers with bounds, products, sums, vectors, refinements), adding mu with Boltzmann sampling when a recursive data needs generating.

L-collaborative-filtering.statement: Use matrix factorization / collaborative filtering to predict an algorithm's runtime on an input.

L-coloneq-act-vs-equiv.statement: := is the act of giving a name a body, while ≡ is the larger relation that follows from all the := plus the computation rules (lambda substitution, recursor rules); "true by definition" broadly means true by unfolding and computing.

L-combine-evidence-refine-certainty.statement: Combine different evidences, different programs running the same function, to refine the certainty in that function.

L-commutative-program.statement: An open question is whether a Luthier program is commutative in the order of its statements, and how to model time/order; declarations can be near-commutative.

L-commuting-squares.statement: Coherence of forgetting and applying functions is analyzed with commuting squares: the two paths are compared for equivalence.

L-compare-equivalent-paths.statement: Luthier compares two paths that do the same thing and determines they are equivalent, possibly with format-conversion stages at the start and end.

L-comparisons-undecidable.statement: Moving off a fixed Float64 makes comparisons undecidable in general (a branch on overlapping intervals has no answer), the most delicate point, met by making decision stability a law.

L-compile-time-prevents-invalid.statement: The type system prevents invalid models from being constructed, eliminating consistency violations at compile time before execution or inference.

L-compiler-is-prover.statement: Letting functions return types makes the Luthier compiler a mathematical prover, so code and its proof become the same thing.

L-compiling-detects-errors.statement: Compiling is checking whether the code holds incompatible things; unlike algebraic calculation, many programs should not compile, because that is how errors are caught.

L-compose-programs.statement: Luthier composes the input and output of one program with another, chaining external programs.

L-compose-programs-harmonically.statement: The fundamental problem is how Luthier programs connect and expand one another so they grow harmonically, with incompatibilities possible.

L-composition-dot.statement: Composition is written with a dot, which explains class methods.

L-compositional-kinetic.statement: Kinetic models are built compositionally from conformational state components as an external product of degrees of freedom with energetic coupling rules and state aggregation.

L-computation-categories.statement: There are categories of computations that take the same time for different inputs, and these classes must be found so not every computation need be measured.

L-computation-for-biology.statement: His student intuition and life's aim is that computation could play for biology the role mathematics played for physics.

L-concept-first.statement: The first step is expressing concepts in Luthier with conceptual depth; the translation/implementation comes after.

L-concept-is-a-function.statement: A concept needs no new type: it is an ordinary function returning a type (with proofs) or a list of laws (with tests).

L-concept-is-predicate-over-functions.statement: A concept is a predicate over functions, a list of requirements, so two implementations satisfying it are interchangeable.

L-concepts-belong-in-luthier.statement: Luthier is where the concepts are expressed, so organizing by Python module instead of by concept was the error that left the central concept (the likelihood) as a black box in Python; the concept must have its own type with its laws inside Luthier.

L-concepts-independent-or-tied.statement: Some concepts can live independently of their container (like a mean) while others are intrinsically tied to one (like an iteration to its algorithm).

L-conceptual-vs-machine-impl.statement: A de novo conceptual implementation stands alongside the machine's, and a conceptual test states and checks their relation (N is isomorphic to the non-negative integers, respecting sum and product), the conceptual definition serving as oracle with the certificate recording the range tested.

L-concrete-to-luthier-problem.statement: A concrete implementation need is used to surface the underlying Luthier design problem.

L-concurrent-session-commit.statement: With another session committing in the same repo, the model leaves its changes uncommitted and first looks at what the other session touched so its work is not swept into a commit with a different message.

L-conjunction-of-predicates.statement: The law wrapper is unneeded; & is conjunction of quantified predicates (X->Bool)->(Y->Bool)->(X*Y->Bool) applied to curried functions, so the law's name is already the quoted expression.

L-constants-must-be-parameters.statement: A criterion hardcoded as a constant in the code (lmMaxIter, the rejection-sampler's try budget) must be a parameter, by the rule that every criterion is a parameter.

L-construction-pattern-is-core.statement: The core of Luthier is one construction pattern: from a material type and a predicate over it derive a certified type, a validating constructor and the forgetful projection to the material, the same for values, functions and whole programs.

L-constructive-reals.statement: Define the reals constructively as Cauchy sequences of rationals with a modulus of convergence, making ℝ's laws testable at finite precision and equality a precision parameter.

L-constructor-vs-function.statement: A constructor differs from a function in that a constructor plus its parameters is the element, making elements transparent, while a function involves a computation.

L-constructors-are-generator.statement: Presenting a type by constructors tied to observers by laws (algebraic ADT spec) makes the constructors the generator, so gen comes free from composing them; without constructors there are no completeness cells.

L-constructors-freely-generated.statement: Constructors of an inductive type are freely generated with no equations, so the Peano disequalities (disjoint, succ injective, succ n distinct from n) are free theorems that survive without definition.

L-constructors-in-type-space.statement: Constructors should live in each type's space rather than in the global space.

L-contagiously-safe-dsl.statement: A compile-time safe model DSL whose safety is contagious, propagating through the system via the compiler, with backend codegen, as the endgame of HoTTification.

L-content-hash-certificate.statement: Content-addressed build: a definition's certificate carries a hash of its elaborated type and body (and its dependency cone), so a matching hash on import satisfies the obligation, files are the source of truth and a relational DB is a reconstructible index.

L-context-as-dag.statement: The program/context is modeled as a Directed Acyclic Graph of definitions where types depend on others, and operating on Luthier is combining DAGs via substitution.

L-contract-bundle.statement: A function's contract bundles its domains, postconditions, comparators, oracles, policies and metadata as one attached object.

L-convergence-law.statement: The Laplace update as a convergence law (departure shrinks with noise at the expected order) measures approximation quality not correctness, so it is not diagnostic and was removed; the optimizer's convergence differs from the approximation's convergence.

L-conversion-syntactic-no-dependent-elim.statement: Conversion is syntactic on neutral terms and there is no dependent elimination, so a type error becomes a pending obligation.

L-core-five-pieces.statement: The core is five pieces (the definition with the hole, lambda calculus with reduction, U, Π, data); from data come Σ, =, ⊥, ⊤, N, Program, while Bayes, the run database and numbers-with-error stay outside as libraries.

L-core-library-sugar-layers.statement: The language is three layers: a small core (a handful of term forms plus data, definition and reduction, a ten-line EBNF with reserved words data, match, extern), a base library written in Luthier, and sugar whose translation is mechanical; no Bool, numbers, =, Sigma or Subtype in the core.

L-core-plus-libraries.statement: Luthier is a closed core plus libraries, the libraries being Luthier functions that connect it to external programs.

L-correlated-data-worth-more.statement: Correlated data are worth more than isolated data, and larger patterns need ever more data.

L-cost-laws.statement: Laws could be extended to go not to a boolean but to a cost: graded cost laws like a generalized unnormalized likelihood, asking how much a value costs rather than whether it complies.

L-couple-to-sonolocalizacion.statement: Luthier is a meta-project whose next development couples to sonolocalización at the library (and MacroIR) stage, and how to relate the two remains to be worked out.

L-coupled-functions-product.statement: When a law couples several functions, the material is their product and the pattern unpacks it to name each component, so the laws are written over named components.

L-couplings-as-types.statement: Energetic couplings, binding schemes and conformational spaces are represented and certified as types.

L-create-objects-uniformly.statement: The language expresses and creates values, variables, types and functions uniformly, with their semantics.

L-criterion-is-cli-hole.statement: A criterion is a hole filled from the command line with --set and recorded in the certificate with the hashes, while effects become externs and luthier run evaluates a main definition.

L-cross-language.statement: Luthier is not tied to one language but a pseudo-language implementable across languages (cross-language, not cross-compiler), with its engine in one and PyLuthier/RLuthier/CLuthier transformable into one another.

L-cross-representation-is-function.statement: A subtype is a restriction within one representation; when two types have different representations their relation is always a certified function with laws, never a subtype, with no implicit coercion (integers injected into the reals do not become reals).

L-cumulative-no-recompute.statement: Luthier is cumulative, never computing the same thing twice except on an explicit override, with knowledge accumulating, perhaps in a relational database.

L-data-gives-recursor.statement: A data declaration gives three things: the type, the constructors (ordinary bodyless functions in normal form), and the recursor (one case per constructor with a reduction rule each); every function over the type is an instance of this recursor.

L-data-sum-of-products.statement: A data is a sum of products plus recursion (sum between constructors, product inside each, recursion as least fixpoint), so data is primitive and + and × are its degenerate cases.

L-data-vs-subtype-choice.statement: Use data when a thing has its own form and operations and a subtype when it is a restriction of something that already has operations; the two are types of equal status and the subtype's short name is the interface.

L-date-both-consolidations.statement: The May consolidation is kept by renaming and dating both versions so the ecosystem's evolution can be compared.

L-declarative-and-executive.statement: Luthier has a declarative part (types that follow laws) and an executive part that runs commands (read a file, execute a function); the executive part can be internal or external.

L-declarative-and-optimizer.statement: Luthier is at once a declarative language and an optimization tool: you declare what you want and it openly shuffles implementations, a map between a declarative language and an executive one.

L-declarative-of-implementation.statement: Luthier needs a declarative description, written in Luthier, of its own implementation: how Luthier code transforms into execution code.

L-declared-vs-defined.statement: A type has states, declared (a forward-declared hole), defined (its invariants given) and certified; a value or extern definition requires a defined type while declarations may reference merely-declared types, which is what builds cyclic definitions.

L-decompose-components.statement: A first task is to understand all the things Luthier currently groups together, to see which are functionally separable and which depend on which.

L-decorator-algebra.statement: Decorators should be easy to express, and one asks whether composing them is associative or commutative, representing the simplest form when it is.

L-decorators-error.statement: Decorators express the error of a number and its propagation (derivatives), as he did in C++ with templates.

L-define-bnf-task.statement: The concrete task is to understand Luthier's syntax and keep a well-defined BNF.

L-define-invariants.statement: Defining an invariant f : A -> B with for-all x : A, g x (f x) where g : A -> B -> Bool: the for-all is the Π, g's Bool is lifted to a proposition via a data Cierto : Bool -> U, and the invariant ties to f either as a separate hole-definition (the declaration is the test) or as a package where the guarantee travels with the function.

L-defined-determined-axes.statement: Defined and determined are independent axes (a hole can have laws without implementation, an extern implementation without laws); a name passes declared, defined, determined, certified.

L-definition-form-depends-on-type.statement: The form of a definition, how its clauses are written, may depend on reducing its type, the same definitional equality at work.

L-definition-fundamental.statement: The most fundamental element of a program is not the type or the function but the definition, name : Type := term; a program is a finite unordered set of definitions and the DAG comes from which names each uses.

L-definition-is-its-test.statement: Defining a function defines its test (its inverse, its simulation), so running the code runs the test.

L-definitional-equality.statement: "True by definition" is definitional equality ≡ (two terms reducing to the same normal form), a judgment the reducer decides, distinct from =, the identity type whose terms are paths, making "the test is the code" literal.

L-delegate-execution.statement: Luthier might delegate execution entirely and do only verification, as extreme minimalism.

L-delegate-representation-python.statement: Luthier expresses the concepts and delegates the representation to Python, with a compiler generating the Python representation now written by hand (the chosen way being to load the .lut at import rather than compile to files), the generated code never edited and carrying the .lut's hash.

L-dep-types-composition.statement: Hierarchical, algebraic model composition across subunits, pathways and scales is enforced by dependent types.

L-dep-types-semantic-safety.statement: Dependent typing enforces semantic safety, guaranteeing the internal consistency of model compositions.

L-dependent-types-as-type-returning.statement: A dependent type is a function that returns a type instead of a value, raising the level of abstraction.

L-dependent-types-basic.statement: Dependent types are probably one of the language's basic initial concepts.

L-dependent-types-def.statement: Dependent types are types that depend on a value, taking the cardinality of that value's type.

L-derived-is-proof-term.statement: A derived object, the tuple of inputs, function, parameters and result, is a proof term whose type is the proposition that the result was obtained that way, making the base a store of proofs.

L-derived-never-edited.statement: A derived object is never edited; corrections are human assertions that are themselves originals, putting labels, quality control and corrections in the same place.

L-description-language.statement: Luthier's first stage is a language for describing the problem, the functions and the conditions under which they work, not for execution.

L-design-approval-before-code.statement: Before implementing anything the model describes the design and waits for approval before writing code.

L-determined-means-reducing-body.statement: A body computes while a law only verifies, so 'determined' in practice means having a body or extern that reduces.

L-determined-up-to-iso.statement: Laws never determine a unique implementation and need not; they make all implementations behave the same from outside, determining the object up to isomorphism.

L-dimension-in-types.statement: The model's dimension must enter the types of probability, belief and optimization (Theta is VecOf n throughout), since with an unconstrained Vec Float64 the model's obligations were false.

L-discrepancy-threshold-cost.statement: A law computes a discrepancy, the theory sets the threshold that makes it Bool, and the use sets the cost, so the theory stays independent of the use.

L-discrete-output-distribution.statement: When a probabilistic path makes the output discrete (a rank, stop reason, count), the result type must be able to say it is a distribution over outcomes.

L-dismantle-prelude.statement: Dismantle the prelude: fundamental is only what the interpreter names on its own while elaborating (Bool, List, Unit/Maybe, Nat), which fits in a twenty-line core, and everything else is a library imported on demand.

L-distinguish-reals-from-float-subtype.statement: Distinguish R, the set of reals, from the Python-implemented subtype (real/Float64), being precise about which is which.

L-do-as-data-dependency.statement: Haskell's do sequencing can be simulated as a data dependency (an output needing an input that doesn't exist yet), so do may not be strictly necessary.

L-do-what-said.statement: The model does what Luciano said and nothing more.

L-dome-gcc-externs.statement: The dome and GCC-PHAT with thousands of samples cannot be native given the speed and will be externs end to end.

L-dot-projection.statement: Since a subtype's component names are public, a field is read with dot notation e.position, pure sugar over a match on the pattern the type declares that needs no new Term constructor and resolves root-level projection name collisions.

L-dot-separator.statement: The dot in Σ (x : X). A x is a notational separator marking where the bound variable ends and the body begins, the same dot as in λ and Π, like the brace in f(x) { ... }, and one convention should serve all three binders.

L-double-definition.statement: A type defined twice could be flagged as error or read as a cartesian product that runs two ways.

L-dsl-as-model-compiler.statement: The DSLs are model compilers that translate high-level mechanistic specifications into executable, inferable structures.

L-dsl-kernel-yaml.statement: A DSL kernel gives a declarative model interface in YAML, isolating the model interface from the C++ internals.

L-dsl-unifies-domains.statement: One DSL framework unifies models across channels, enzymes, networks, signaling and regulation.

L-dynamic-naming.statement: For dynamically created types or functions, a name is really an address, so a generated numeric identifier suffices.

L-easy-delegation.statement: Delegation should be easy in Luthier, an idea he traces to Modelica.

L-effects-as-threaded-pointers.statement: The external world is a type that exists and nothing constructs, with no equality, whose values are pointers externs give, threaded linearly so their order lives in the graph of definitions and a reused pointer is a type error.

L-el-reading.statement: El abbreviates elements: El c reads as the elements of what the code c names.

L-el-vs-typeof-naming.statement: typeOf would mislead since typeOf c means Code, not the type c names; for Luthier the decoder is named Decode, pairing with Code.

L-elegant-vs-mosaic.statement: A language is elegant when its constructions follow from one or two ideas and its self-interpreter fits a page, mosaic when each construction was added for a need; Luthier's spec is elegant but the interpreter has mosaic pieces the next round should remove.

L-element-belongs-one-type.statement: Each element belongs to exactly one type but can serve to build many types.

L-embedded-semantic-structure.statement: Biological models carry embedded semantic structure such as symmetry groups, compositional operators and equivalence classes.

L-encode-as-types.statement: Model components, entities and deterministic structure are encoded as types.

L-encode-epistemic-structure.statement: Scientific code should encode its epistemic structure as executable epistemology, with verification semantic rather than syntactic and type safety arising from epistemic clarity.

L-environment-evaluator.statement: Luthier's evaluator should use environments and closures so each argument and constant is computed once (concepts are unique), replacing substitution which copies the body and recomputes multiply-used arguments.

L-environment-first-object.statement: The environment is the first object the language must define, since data is loaded into it.

L-environment-kinds.statement: There are simple environments (one value type, one identifier) and compound ones that admit multiple.

L-environment-resources.statement: The environment needs and manages resources (memory and compute) and function execution, a problem that ties to it but exceeds it (OS, compiler).

L-environment-stores-retrieves.statement: The environment is a map of definitions whose two mechanisms are storing and retrieving variables by name.

L-epistemic-compression.statement: A few adjunction-derived tests cover most of the risk; verification is compressed into a minimal, epistemically meaningful suite.

L-epistemic-firewall.statement: The SAV verification layer acts as an epistemic firewall defending the system against silent semantic drift during refactoring.

L-equalities-should-be-setoid.statement: Loose equalities like BeliefFamily.same and Codec.eq should be Setoid instances.

L-equality-check-holes.statement: R8 has holes: == is accepted over data containing functions, over Real as float equality, and not checked past depth 20.

L-equality-parametrized-probability.statement: Objects are parametrized by observational equality and eventually by a probability of being equal or distinct, where equality returns a verdict with its level rather than a Bool.

L-equality-symbols.statement: Equality gets distinct symbols: := defines (an asymmetric act), = is the identity type (the proposition), == is library decidable equality, and ≡, the definitional one, is not written in programs.

L-equals-assertion.statement: The equals sign is an assertion that both sides are equal, also used for pattern matching when a symbol is unknown.

L-ergonomics-let-unary-minus.statement: Writing costs for lack of let, implicit arguments and unary minus (functions end in ten closing braces), which should come before any kernel refinement.

L-error-is-failing-predicate.statement: An error is a predicate that fails, represented by a single recursive type Failure, a tree of label, argument and sub-failures whose labels are quotes of program terms, the same structure as the success certificate, which only a language where code is data can build.

L-error-messages-remembering.statement: Luthier must produce well-structured error messages, the remembering of why one erred, returning the failed sub-graph with each node's trace.

L-essential-vs-decoration.statement: Function equivalences separate what is essential (the equivalent) from what is decoration (efficiency, cost), the non-equivalent.

L-ev-sugar-syntax.statement: The sugar that stores an evaluation needs delimiters and always stores, since the context cannot decide its type and keeping only failures is the test's filter, not a property of the evaluation.

L-eval-fuel.statement: eval repeating a step is not structural recursion and need not terminate, so it is given fuel, eval : N -> Program -> Term -> Maybe Term, making it total, and how much fuel was needed is the first cost measure for free.

L-eval-modes.statement: You define a program and ask to execute/eval it under different modified evaluations (with test, with extensive test, copying everything that happens); having several execution modes is the attraction of such a language.

L-evaluation-steps-memory-states.statement: Evaluation is represented by the states of memory (2; 2+; 2+2; 4), possibly with pointers to a partially applied function, with syntax, range and type errors (arcsin of a string, a value out of range) caught along the way.

L-evaluation-storage-object.statement: The object storing a function, its argument and its result is the graph of evaluation (Ev f), with a sugar that evaluates and stores it; evalstore is just that pair, not a third operation, and the run base is a list of them.

L-evidence-in-sigma.statement: Being more specific with types means types are data and knowledge about a value is carried as an evidence component in a Σ, marked erasable, but with the evidence sometimes written and kept and the erasable mark set by whoever defines.

L-exception-skips-obligation.statement: A type obligation speaks of the values a computation produces, so an exception yields no value and that case is skipped, whereas a law stated in a definition's type keeps failing on an exception.

L-executable-by-hand.statement: If well written, Luthier should be executable by hand with pencil and paper, like Lisp.

L-execute-when-defined.statement: Code is not executed until it is fully defined, so undefined dead code can sit there without bothering anyone.

L-execution-as-forgetting.statement: Execution is a forgetful function: code generates code, with one level that keeps the generated code and one that forgets it.

L-execution-is-verification.statement: Execution in Luthier is the verification of equivalences, as mathematics does not execute but only verifies equivalences.

L-executive-code-in-luthier.statement: One must be able to write the executive code itself in Luthier.

L-exhaustive-int-is-small-range.statement: "Exhaustive" over Int means only the range -16 to 16, so a law is certified exhaustive on 33 cases that are not exhaustive.

L-expansion-synthesis-cycle.statement: The work expands before it contracts: one idea generates many and then synthesis reaches a richer core, a breathing cycle of expansion and synthesis.

L-experiment-zero-independent.statement: experiment_zero does not depend on distances; it uses its own model over the whole position vector, with distances a separate branch.

L-explicit-error-types.statement: Errors should be explicit types rather than Maybe_error over a string, and the error sum E1+E2 is an ordinary type the verifier computes, neither dynamic nor dependent, with Maybe_error being the maximally forgotten Failure.

L-express-alternatives.statement: The point is not to do everything but to have the tools to express different alternatives; no option is best or worst, and even expressing something to discard it has value.

L-express-extracomputational.statement: The language expresses extra-computational concepts like probability by abstracting their properties and verifying compliance (e.g. a probability lies in [0,1]).

L-express-invariances.statement: Luthier's aim is to express the invariances of the disciplines (a species mates within itself; electrons are fermions, photons bosons).

L-express-math-structures.statement: The language must express mathematical structures (category, functor, group) with their laws, possibly in several declaration styles.

L-express-then-execute.statement: You first express the ideas with pencil and paper and then go to execution or the empirical database; these are two layers, not opposed philosophies.

L-expressiveness.statement: Code must express its intention to both the human reader and the compiler, referring truthfully to known structures.

L-expressivity-vs-redundancy.statement: A choice between redundancy (robustness) and expressivity; he prefers expressivity with good compiler messages, since redundancy can needlessly limit.

L-extensionality-law.statement: An extensionality law (two values equal when all observers agree) is what turns 'the same observations' into 'the same object'.

L-exterior-is-files.statement: What is outside Luthier is largely files (executables, Python code, data, plots, even sensors), plus mutable memory, resources and processors.

L-extern-gives-value-not-type.statement: An extern always gives a value, never a type (pyTable : Table .= extern, not Table := extern); when a Python value represents a native type the boundary is a certified representation translation.

L-extern-is-labeled-hole.statement: extern is a hole with a label saying who fills it, the border between what runs and what does not, possibly an ordinary library function rather than a keyword.

L-extern-provisional-qualifier.statement: A qualifier (extern provisional) lets an extern stand over a not-yet-defined type in a rush, recording the debt in the certificate.

L-external-element.statement: Everything that is not Luthier (C++, Python, the machine, any resource) is modeled as its own kind of external element.

L-failure-mass-sampling.statement: What n passing sampled cases update is the failure mass theta under the usage distribution, not the law's truth, with a Beta prior giving Beta(a,b+n), theta of order 1/n, composing by union bound and transferring between uses through the saved posterior.

L-few-rich-concepts-analyzable.statement: A synthesis of few but rich concepts can be judged for sense; when it grows long with ideas he doesn't command it distracts and distorts until he doubts everything.

L-field-laws-pass-by-tuned-magnitude.statement: The field laws of float64Field pass only because lawMagnitude is tuned to the generator range; associativity fails at (1e8, -1e8, 3e-9) and the type does not state the box.

L-file-is-sigma-value.statement: A .lut file denotes a value of a Sigma type with named components like Ring, so a library's signature is its type, two interchangeable libraries are two values of one type, and a parametrized library is a module-to-module function.

L-files-as-interface.statement: What remains after running are files and pdfs, and the human interface is reading comprehensible files, perhaps json.

L-fin-int-vs-machine.statement: Fin n is semantically the finite set over ℤ; a machine integer is not another definition of Fin but a representation of a subset of ℤ, written as two presentations with an equivalence law.

L-first-class-contexts.statement: The context could be treated as a type in itself, what theory calls first-class contexts.

L-fisher-validation.statement: A likelihood implementation is validated by agreement between the Fisher Information Matrix from score covariance and the one from the Hessian, without full inference.

L-fix-certification-as-gate.statement: Freeze v0 and commit, then fix certification as a gate (generators respecting refinements, pending distinct from failure, delete entries without a current name, record the uncertified cone).

L-fixpoint-generation-cost.statement: Generating a value of a fixpoint needs termination control: the cost is the size and the per-size counts come from the code without looking at a value, under the same accumulated-cost rule as numbers and censuses.

L-float64-refines-real.statement: Float64 is written as a refinement of the real type (Float64 : Real := primitive), each finite double being a real.

L-folds-are-monoid-fold.statement: The folds over Fin n (sumTo, totalDef, maxOver, forallBelow, listLength) are all the same monoid fold and should be one right-associated fold.

L-forgetful-functors.statement: Which forgetting function you apply to the types defines the language you speak; forgetful functors are among Luthier's most important components, and different ones optimize different things.

L-forgetting-affects-precision.statement: How much of the operational history is kept determines the recoverable numerical precision, tying the forget functor to precision.

L-forgetting-in-hott.statement: The concept of forgetting (a type forgetting parts of the type) is already present in HoTT.

L-forgetting-is-fst.statement: Forgetting is fst of a Σ, and what to forget is library policy.

L-forgetting-problem.statement: The forgetting problem, controlling the typing information that grows as types compose, is one of Luthier's fundamental problems to solve.

L-form-before-laws.statement: A type's form, its base and labels, must be fixed in the declaration before its laws, since laws are written over its components and typed before the type closes.

L-formalize-state-energy-algebra.statement: Planned work to formalize a type system for state and energy algebra and HoTT-based state composition primitives.

L-formers-are-primitive.statement: Elementary types and functions are not primitive; the primitives are the formers (U, Π, data), with N defined by data, R a structure with axioms and seno a hole.

L-forms-of-definition.statement: The language distinguishes declaration from definition and lets one define functions or variables by their type without giving the implementation or value (parameters).

L-forward-and-undefined-types.statement: A type may be referenced before it is defined and defined later, or left undefined, in which case it is a program input.

L-foundation-choice.statement: Open question of which foundation to build on (type theory vs category theory, HoTT vs ZMT).

L-full-to-unprovable.statement: What distinguishes Luthier is carrying types-as-propositions a full to propositions that cannot be proved, so the grade of verification must be part of what belonging to a type affirms.

L-function-as-expected-loss.statement: What is left of a function is an expected loss, a posterior characterization that must be processable, expressible as a type of generator, test and cost.

L-function-by-properties.statement: A function can be defined by its properties, the propositions its inputs and outputs satisfy, not only operationally, keeping both.

L-function-deterministic.statement: If the identity of a derived object is its inputs, function, version and parameters, the function must be deterministic: seed and environment enter as explicit arguments, or the certificate lies.

L-function-generators-degenerate.statement: Function generators are degenerate, so any law quantified over functions is tested on a degenerate sample.

L-function-holds-code.statement: A function holds its code written in the language plus a compiled simplified form.

L-function-kinds.statement: Functions are of two kinds: predefined and user defined.

L-function-subtyping-float64.statement: The function subtyping rule (domain contravariant, codomain covariant) accepts the argument and promotes the Float64 a leaf returns to Real, with an explicit toFloat64 where a Real must be rounded.

L-function-type-expression.statement: Open question of how to express the type of a function such as write : a -> string.

L-functions-by-hand-cheaper.statement: Against his own argument: the same verified functions could be written by hand without the whole Luthier apparatus.

L-functions-need-no-self-knowledge.statement: Functions need no self-knowledge; a law is an ordinary function to Bool and the label is put by the verifier level, which knows the whole program and runs test as an operation over Program.

L-functor-as-implementation.statement: A functor is read as an implementation and a natural transformation as translating one implementation into another.

L-fundamental-elements-question.statement: What are the most fundamental elements of a program? Candidates: elementary types, elementary functions, code versus data, true/false, true-by-definition, address/data.

L-gap-of-usefulness.statement: The method is to find the gap of usefulness, a concrete place from which Luthier can begin to develop while being useful.

L-gen-over-refined-type.statement: A generator is defined only over a type with a predicate, so a type like BrokenGraph must be a refinement subtype whose predicate the generated values are checked against.

L-generalize-database.statement: The performance database must be generalizable from point measurements to trends, e.g. estimating an empty cell from its row and column averages or something more sophisticated.

L-generated-code-not-real.statement: He is stuck because the model generates Luthier code that to him is not code, since he cannot tell whether it meets Luthier's real norms.

L-generated-value-checked-against-type.statement: Each value a registered generator produces is checked against its type and a value outside it is an error, with gen T trusted as the declared-trust escape.

L-generation-part-of-certificate.statement: Unless a gen is declared the tester builds values from the type's structure, and that construction is part of what each certificate means and silently decides what a law actually tests; generators are checked for being in the type, never for covering it.

L-generator-explicit-per-type.statement: There is no single generator per type, so a test must name the explicit generator it bound to each type and the certificate records it (gen T := disappears); functions are generated by a census over registered values.

L-generator-ignores-refinement.statement: The generator does not respect dependent refinements, producing false failures because the obligation was quantified over the base type, not the refined one.

L-generator-is-luthier-value.statement: A generator is a Luthier value with its own type and laws, certifiable like any other, and the random number generator is an extern with its stochasticity laws declared in Luthier.

L-generator-magnitude.statement: A depth-bounded generator only reaches small numbers, so size is a test parameter growing from 1 to a cap along the cases, and a generator that returns a refined type carries its own law and travels certified.

L-generators-plan-not-implemented.statement: The most serious issue is that the whole generators plan is not implemented and may not even be specified.

L-generic-concept-contextualized.statement: A concept like status or iteration can be a generic class, with the particular algorithm it belongs to known from its containing context and carried as an identifier.

L-generic-functor-in-interpreter.statement: Generic functors live in the interpreter, derived from the type's structure as == already is, named and recorded in the certificate but not written in Luthier.

L-generic-functor-needs-reflection.statement: Generators as values and generics as functors over the type contradict, since a functor over any type would need (T:U)->Gen T and reflection over types, which Luthier lacks.

L-generic-laws-dont-run.statement: Laws generic in a type parameter (Theta : U) never run because there is no generator of U, so they are certified only when a program fills the hole with a concrete type that has a generator, or by a well-chosen instance, and asking for a generator of U is a static error.

L-generic-vs-project-location.statement: Generic libraries live in luthier/lib and project-specific files in sonolocalización, ending the duplicated copies that caused confusion.

L-genuine-dependence.statement: The predicates connecting a type's components must be genuinely dependent and non-separable; a fake f(x,y)=g(x) should not count, and a separability failure needs a witnessed verdict.

L-grammar-parallel.statement: Natural-language grammatical categories parallel programming constructs, a frame for choosing Luthier's primitives.

L-graph-ends-types-middle-trace.statement: The whole thing is a graph with the situated-object types at the ends and inference running over the Python trace in the middle.

L-groupoid-structure.statement: Inference operations and their diagnostics form equivalence classes, a pre-formal groupoid structure.

L-guarantees-in-comments.statement: Guarantees live in comments instead of in types (meanModel says its inputs are nodes but MapInput carries Vec Int unrelated to Node).

L-hardcode-twice-across-bridge.statement: Fixed facts like the gauge nodes are written twice across the Python/Luthier bridge, breaking one-name-per-thing and the no-hardcoding rule.

L-hardwired-names-interpreter.statement: There are hardwired names in the interpreter, so Fin is recognized only by name and an alias of Fin loses its array representation and memoization.

L-hash-compared-after-holes-filled.statement: Certificate hashes are compared at the end of loading with the holes filled, a library with holes being a structure with parameters whose laws are certified per filling.

L-hidden-parameter-exposed.statement: A hidden parameter that affects the guarantee, like a max depth with no criterion, must be recorded in the certificate and exposed.

L-higher-paths-symmetries.statement: Higher-order symmetries and transformations between equivalences are captured as higher paths.

L-hijack-code.statement: Luthier must be able to hijack code from any other language.

L-hole-five-roles.statement: The hole, a definition with a type and no body, plays five roles at once (axiom, program input, external function, pending definition, dead code), and "you don't execute until it's defined" is its exact semantics, removing the need for an External type.

L-hole-goal-messages.statement: A hole inside a term lets the verifier accept what is written and state the exact type of what is missing (Agda's goal), which is the compiler with good messages about what is happening.

L-hole-needs-no-symbol.statement: The hole needs no symbol in the core: a bodyless declaration f : A → B is already a hole, an opaque name that doesn't reduce, and ? is derivable surface sugar.

L-hole-no-default.statement: In Luthier a hole has no default, so each run must supply every parameter by --set; a parameter with a default value that --set replaces and the run records would be a new language feature.

L-hole-no-intention.statement: The core does not distinguish why a hole has no body (to be filled externally or just unwritten); huecos : Program → List Name lists them all and intention goes in the definition's text field.

L-hook-only-changed-files.statement: A Stop hook that runs luthier check over all project files charges every turn; it should run only on changed .lut files.

L-host-minimal-duties.statement: If the interpreter is written in Luthier the host need only reduce, run the primitive types' operations, and call an extern reading and writing a File, plus read a canonical serialization of Term, with everything else Luthier definitions over Program.

L-hot-values-paths.statement: Hot values open a larger universe of possible paths than ordinary values.

L-hott-dsl-for-biology.statement: Build a domain-specific modeling language on Homotopy Type Theory for expressing, composing and transforming biological models with access to type-level structure.

L-hott-ingredients-sufficient.statement: Sigma-types, Pi-types, identity types and HITs suffice to encode conformational models, energetic couplings and symmetry structures.

L-hott-not-probabilistic.statement: HoTT does not work on probabilities, though probabilities could be built within it; the defect is that it is not native.

L-hott-prob-tension.statement: There is a tension between HoTT's invertible identities and univalence and probability's non-invertible uncertainty, with no fully unified model yet.

L-hottification-definition.statement: HoTTification is transforming a scientific model, algorithm or modeling language into a formal structure governed by HoTT, analogous to categorification or quantization.

L-hottification-models-typed-objects.statement: Under HoTTification models themselves become typed mathematical objects whose equivalences, symmetries and compositions are validated by the type system.

L-hottification-roadmap.statement: HoTTification is a staged program, a semantic elevation not a rewrite, running from SAV diagnostics through DSL/CLI modularization and wrappers to a full homotopical, type-theoretic kernel.

L-idea-affects-world-when-executed.statement: Ideas are free and don't affect the world until executed, when they can affect it enormously; some ideas have enormous power.

L-idea-as-infective-virus.statement: A powerful idea is like a more infective virus that also organizes, by analogy with the cell nucleus being a virus that appropriates the cell and leaves something better.

L-identifier-type-independent.statement: The identifier and the type are completely independent; the identifier is a fantasy name unknown until resolved.

L-identifiers-central.statement: Identifiers are central: a simple label recovers a complex object, the dictionary joining human and machine.

L-identity-paths-equivalences.statement: Identity paths represent structural equivalences between model entities.

L-implementation-of-concept.statement: A Luthier definition should determine uniquely that a concrete computation is an implementation of a concept (e.g. of matrices).

L-implicit-type-params.statement: Implicit type parameters are deduced by unification at application, so an unannotated lambda is checked after deducing its type from the other argument.

L-implicit-types.statement: Types can be defined implicitly, as the solution to a problem or the optimum of a function, rather than declared directly.

L-import-declares-dependencies.statement: A .lut file declares its dependencies with import, which is the combinar operation (union of definitions rejecting conflicts), with a prefix form to disambiguate clashing names.

L-indexat-nat.statement: An index typed Int admits negatives and makes an obligation genuinely false, so the honest type for an index is Nat.

L-indexed-data-families.statement: Indexed constructors whose return type carries an index (Vec : N -> U) are a further layer of data, letting a type like Traza t u have constructors only for pairs that really reduce to one another.

L-infectability-lens.statement: Consolidation uses infectability as its lens: the ideas that most change how you program are the ones that most structure the language; it is a project-specific choice.

L-inject-multiple-identifiers.statement: A type or function can inject more than one identifier into the environment.

L-int-overflow-numpy-bridge.statement: Int in the interpreter is unbounded ℤ (Python int) but becomes int64 on crossing to numpy with no check, a silent-overflow source the spec and bridge must name.

L-int-real-string-primitive.statement: Int, R and String are an unavoidable exception as core primitives, since defining IEEE double with data makes no sense.

L-int-tables-as-float.statement: Fin n -> Int tables are generated as float64 against spec 06, so integer laws over indices run with floating-point division.

L-intermediate-ai-scale.statement: Is there an intermediate scale where the AI multiplies the author's effort without the result ceasing to be legible and checkable by him?

L-interpreted-likelihood-slow.statement: A 30-parameter fit takes 3 minutes because the cost is the interpreted likelihood.

L-interpreter-hash-recertify-cost.statement: Including the interpreter's fingerprint in the hash means any interpreter fix invalidates every certificate, forcing recertification in batches.

L-interval-arithmetic-bounded-real.statement: Interval arithmetic fits Luthier because its correctness is a single inclusion law Luthier can already certify: a bounded Real is a certificate carried across a computation that yields a bound for a function's values.

L-interval-enclosure-law.statement: With an interval model the approximation law is stated once for any f as enclosure (f_Float64 x ∈ f_Interval x), so the tolerance is computed in test rather than chosen by hand.

L-invariant-definition.statement: An invariant is something that does not change whatever happens.

L-invariant-is-bool-function-field.statement: In version 0 an invariant is a function returning Bool, stored as a field of the definition beside the body, with a generator hole filled by type and the run kept as data.

L-invariants-as-laws-predicates.statement: Invariants are represented by laws, and laws are predicates (statements that something holds, is feasible, is positive).

L-inventory-cpp-constructs.statement: An inventory of C++ constructs (classes, functions, enums, structs, templates, pointers, references, derived classes, polymorphism) as what exists and must be selected from.

L-inverse-cdf-sampling.statement: Sampling by the cumulative sum of costs is inverse-CDF sampling, one primitive for the continuous case (linear or log) and the finite census, with exhaustive over an infinite type a static error.

L-invert-arrow-registration.statement: Invert the arrow so the .lut declares a hole with its signature and the environment (sonolik) fills it by registration, instead of signatures coming from what Python already has.

L-io-codec-prism.statement: Luthier separates the IO effect (a law-less extern) from the format, a pure codec of parse and render with round-trip laws, which is a prism, the partial version of Iso.

L-is-it-a-dsl.statement: In implementation Luthier is a DSL in Python, and only a few things justify a separate language: the judgment that a value satisfies a type, the certificate as persistent composable evidence, the hole as a first-class citizen, environment independence, and a future fifth of proving rather than testing.

L-iteration-as-successor.statement: An iteration is defined by construction, applying a step that increments a successor, and the successor applies to sets beyond the naturals.

L-iteration-propagation.statement: Data-length iteration (MCMC and the like) is the common case, and what must be designed is its three forms of propagation, cut at first fail, accumulate, and decorate, with the forget functor keeping the decoration from overwhelming the value.

L-judgment-depends-on-type.statement: a : A is a judgment, not a proposition, and what it means depends on the kind of type A is (a mere proposition: A holds and a is how I know; a set: a is one of A's elements).

L-juxtaposition-application.statement: Application is written by juxtaposition f a and binds tighter than any operator, so f(a) is the same, f a b is curried and f (a, b) applies to a pair, the two coexisting as distinct types, with multiplication explicit.

L-keep-witness-high-information.statement: Since these functions are expensive, keep the witness that a function worked or failed, giving priority to high-information values far from the prior (the unexpected ones).

L-kernel-choice-criterion.statement: The canonical core is chosen not by minimality but so the static semantics can be stated directly on it without a translation, keeping the subtype primitive though derivable.

L-kernel-triangle-works.statement: The Kernel triangle with two controls, each breaking a different side, is among what works.

L-know-that-vs-which.statement: The distinction to keep is knowing that (a mere proposition's proof) versus knowing which (a set's value); the passage from the second to the first is truncation, the most basic forgetting, where the forget functor begins.

L-knowledge-butler.statement: The ideal is to use Luthier alongside the AI as a kind of butler of knowledge.

L-knowledge-ties-parts.statement: What ties the declarative and executive parts is knowledge: the program holds propositions and updates them by what it executes.

L-knowledge-vs-certificate.statement: Certified is knowledge not a state of the name, so the record splits into knowledge (the posterior over a model's behavior given prior, model class and evidence, joined across runs) and certificate (a decision for a use, a query over that knowledge that must not write the posterior's mode as a fact).

L-knuth-expressive-languages.statement: Luthier draws the most expressive and natural from lambda calculus, Lisp, C++ and Python, aiming at a language Knuth would like, with code as a first-class citizen.

L-labels-are-binders.statement: Record labels are binding names like parameter names, so they do not enter the type's identity; a labelled record and the bare product are the same type.

L-language-for-the-ai.statement: Luthier should be a language used by the AI itself, with the risk that it self-hacks.

L-language-forces-method.statement: Luthier's relevance is forcing the author and the AI to be methodical, and a program that compiles gives some assurance it is not garbage, by analogy with Lean's proofs.

L-language-indicates-knowledge.statement: Luthier is thought of as a language that indicates knowledge, in Martin-Löf's reading where a judgment is an act of knowledge and the bodyless hole is an epistemic assumption.

L-language-is-universe.statement: Inventing a programming language is like inventing a universe with its own laws.

L-language-of-ideas.statement: Luthier is a language for defining ideas, where ideas are first-class citizens, like natural languages define things.

L-language-parts-compiler.statement: The language has parts: a grammar with semantic rules and a front compiler to C++.

L-language-self-writing.statement: Defining new types and functions should itself be programmable, the language writing itself, which requires a simple robust language with no syntactic sugar.

L-languages-from-theory.statement: Popular languages are not better founded; now that metatheory can be machine-verified an old language can end up better founded than a new one, and Luthier is on the side born from a theory.

L-law-as-object-classifier.statement: A law need not return Bool: its codomain can be an object classifier with an order and a 'holds' element (a quantale Omega, the positive reals as a cost, or the universe U of evidence types), the theory being the sublevel set under a threshold and Bool the case {0,infinity}.

L-law-characterizes-not-reimplements.statement: A law states the mathematical property that determines an operation up to the presentation's equality; a second implementation is consistency not characterization, and the native definition is one more model certified against it.

L-law-in-hole-declaration.statement: The law belongs in the hole's declaration so filling it with the extern inherits the obligation and every use of the name is a certified value, removing the duplicated certified copies.

L-law-independence-witnessed.statement: A law is independent if a model exists satisfying all the others and violating it, an existential needing the witnessed verdict.

L-law-is-type-plus-predicate.statement: A law is a type of arguments together with a predicate over them, so the generator knows what to sample and different laws can quantify over different variables.

L-law-needs-concrete-case.statement: As Luthier preaches for code, a law is written first but holds only when a concrete case puts it to the test.

L-law-needs-enough-operands.statement: A law like associativity only becomes testable once enough variables are derived (three numbers for associativity), so the system must record which were derived to know when a law can be checked.

L-law-only-when-known-true.statement: A hole-filled program is valid and the complete .lut is the specification; a law is written only when already known true (by math or existing tests), since an unverified law that turns out false is worse than a hole.

L-law-takes-function-as-argument.statement: A law takes the function under test as its first argument and the quantified variables after, so the type it belongs to has any implementation as a term.

L-law-verification-puzzle.statement: Verifying a law is like fitting a puzzle: the law relates all elements at once, so checking it means computing cases and seeing whether the pieces cohere.

L-laws-are-declarations.statement: Laws are ordinary declarations, holes until proven, and falsifiable by an instance that does not type.

L-laws-are-the-normal-form.statement: The novelty is that a group of functions with its laws, as a type whose laws are run by default, is the normal way to define anything, not a separate verification tool.

L-laws-didnt-need-language.statement: The four laws that paid off are well chosen but none needed the language; they come out the same with pytest plus hypothesis.

L-laws-force-decisions.statement: Writing a group's laws forces design decisions, such as what a read of an absent key returns.

L-laws-hypergraph-connected.statement: Connection is a property of the whole set of laws: the hypergraph of laws must be connected and cover all components.

L-laws-like-cpp-requires.statement: Laws are written in few lines like a C++ requires block: quantified variables in a header and one Bool expression per line, each a type requirement checked without running or a value requirement run by the test.

L-laws-live-in-type.statement: Laws live in the type and thus in the DAG like any definition, so changing a law invalidates dependents' certificates through the graph, and laws can be shared, cross components, or be inherited by a subtype over a subtype.

L-laws-of-interpretation-steps.statement: Luthier should carry the laws of each interpretation step (reduce, apply), written in Luthier, so one can check that Luthier's precepts hold; with apply and reduce almost all of it is done.

L-leaf-declared-over-float64.statement: An extern leaf is declared over what it really receives and returns (Vec Float64, not Real), since the type cannot affirm what the implementation does not deliver, forcing libraries generic in the number type.

L-leaf-not-certified-via-another-leaf.statement: A leaf's certification tolerance should use the native definition, not another leaf, so no leaf certifies itself by leaning on another.

L-learn-from-each-run.statement: From each run of the code something is learned, whether an implementation is correct or how fast it is.

L-levels-of-equivalence.statement: A fundamental idea of Luthier is to express different levels of equivalence (same information, isomorphic, exactly equal, same memory location), each a different equivalence functor.

L-levels-of-verification.statement: A value can be untested or tested, with different levels of verification.

L-levels-of-view.statement: From a series of operations one can take different views or levels: the magma, the result, the execution, the code.

L-library-adapter.statement: A library is used by requiring it follow patterns and satisfy propositions defined from Luthier, with an adapter fitting it to each use, so Luthier acts as a universal adapter between libraries.

L-likelihood-tangent-dimension.statement: Likelihood does not carry the dimension of its tangent space, so a density pair declared over the whole vector asserted something false and is restated over the dimensioned domain.

L-likelihood-type-propagation.statement: Likelihood recursion is encoded via type-theoretic propagation, with noise structures and model boundaries as dependent types.

L-lisp-quote-code-as-data.statement: Writing f a as data within a program uses the Lisp quote '(f a) as sugar, with the parser producing the Term constructors.

L-lisp-single-primitive.statement: Lisp reduces everything to one primitive, lists, as inspiration for reducing Luthier.

L-literal-lint-type-vs-criterion.statement: A mechanical criterion to classify numeric literals: a constant in type position (a refinement bound) defines a type, one in term position is a criterion.

L-living-vs-dead-language.statement: Luthier can be a living language that acts or a dead language that only describes; the descriptive role is where it starts.

L-lm-controls-excluded.statement: The Levenberg-Marquardt controls were excluded on purpose because they belong to this particular case.

L-luciano-writes-interpreter-c.statement: Once the syntax is fixed, Luciano would write the Luthier interpreter himself, eventually a small core in C for speed with the rest in Luthier.

L-lut-first-then-python.statement: Develop the whole .lut program first and do the Python implementation afterward.

L-luthier-costs-more-than-returns.statement: As a design Luthier improved this week, but as a sonolocalización tool it today costs the project more than it returns.

L-luthier-describe-deal-inverted.statement: The handoff deal that Luthier only describes got inverted; now gauge, jacobian, model and native solvers live in Luthier and Python must match it bit for bit.

L-luthier-describes-python-works.statement: In this phase Luthier only describes (types, laws, extern, test) with no non-trivial function bodies, and Python does the work.

L-luthier-fills-need.statement: Can Luthier fill an existing need and let one express things not expressible in other languages?

L-luthier-is-assignments.statement: Luthier is a chain of assignments, each an identifier, an equals sign and an operation that creates the object.

L-luthier-is-extended-concepts.statement: Luthier is C++ concepts extended to the whole language: predicates with semantic requirements that are run and whose results are stored, keeping subsumption and composition.

L-luthier-is-verified-library.statement: Luthier itself is a series of verified types and functions with their theorems and tests, almost an instance of the pattern.

L-luthier-reflection-question.statement: Luciano challenges the claim that Luthier has no reflection over types.

L-luthier-runs-and-tests.statement: Luthier both runs and tests, becoming the legible documentation of a Python project, with leaves in Python that iterate over data and composition in Luthier that iterates over concepts, so a program that runs is its documentation.

L-luthier-self-presentations.statement: Luthier itself admits different equivalent primitive elements and laws (it already has several presentations of itself, with sugar-to-core a translation), and one must be chosen.

L-luthier-states-not-programs.statement: Luthier should be a language to state and certify the claims of a computation done in Python or R, not a language to program in.

L-luthier-types-python-values.statement: Luthier provides only the types with their postconditions and laws; the values are external, instantiated extern in Python, and no extern is declared U.

L-luthier-v0-limits.statement: Luthier v0 cannot express expectations, certify a concrete run, or handle objects that are files, so stages that need those stay typed holes; that boundary is Luthier's limit, named as a gap in what was built.

L-luthierize-foreign-code.statement: Luthier annotates and 'luthierizes' foreign code, verifying it against the definition of what it should do within some error.

L-machine-verifiable-theories.statement: HoTTification offers a path toward machine-verifiable biological theories.

L-macroir-consumes-models.statement: MacroIR consumes structurally defined Markov models and computes interval-averaged likelihoods for macroscopic current data.

L-many-function-types.statement: A function's type need not be unique; there can be many function types one invents, such as positive functions from reals to positive reals.

L-map-as-iterate.statement: The MAP is assembled from a step function and an is_finished predicate via a generic iterate_until driver that separates algorithm from model, with an optimization module whose laws take the implementation as argument.

L-map-invariants.statement: Proposed invariants that certify the MAP (covariance calibration, null score, exact Hessian, rigid motion, scale, permutations, prior limits, and more).

L-map-to-other-languages.statement: Describe functions and equivalences and map them to other languages (C, C++, Java), not directly but by giving the tools for others to extend the translation.

L-markov-generated.statement: Markov models become generated objects rather than arbitrary inputs.

L-match-is-recursor-sugar.statement: match is not primitive but sugar for the recursor a data declaration gives, the only way to open a data value, and over Bool it is if.

L-materialization-cache-bug.statement: The materialization cache keyed only by id(f) returns incorrect results, a correctness bug not a performance one.

L-math-concept-stack.statement: The statistical objects are a bottom-up stack of mathematical concepts as types (measurable space, measure, density as Radon-Nikodym derivative, Markov kernel, expectation as positive linear functional, inner product), with Fisher information the inner product of L squared restricted to the tangent space and the gaussian model a map between inner-product spaces.

L-mechanical-check-is-shadow.statement: Rules that are matters of judgment transfer to a mechanical check only as a substitute, a shadow of the real rule.

L-mechanical-rules-plan-consistency.statement: Luciano doubts whether the mechanical-rules plan is consistent.

L-mechanize-rules-lint-hook.statement: The instructions living in memory are moved to mechanical checks in three layers (what Luthier can reject, what a repo lint catches, what stays judgment with a mechanical reminder), which requires relaxing the rule that only Luciano runs the scripts for lints and certification.

L-membership-construction-or-hypothesis.statement: A value belongs to a type either by construction (the case is given) or by hypothesis, a construction by value that can fail.

L-mentor-friction.statement: The mentor step produces friction on the design process without designing itself.

L-meta-layer.statement: The language sits as a meta-layer above the ConformationalModel DSL, MacroIR and Bayesian pipelines.

L-meta-recursive.statement: The object of Luthier is to work on Luthier; being meta-recursive, operating on itself from the start, is fundamental.

L-meta-theory-discovery.statement: The final product is a meta-theory of scientific discovery architecture, a unifiable theory-building system, not just new models.

L-minimal-core-primitives.statement: There should be a clear core where all Luthier operations execute, with only a few primitives implemented in C or similar so it runs.

L-minimal-primitives.statement: Open question whether Luthier needs primitive functions or only coordinates external ones, keeping native components minimal, perhaps only identity and equality.

L-minimalism-maximalism.statement: There is no contradiction between minimalism and maximalism: the minimalism is in the few founding components, from which a huge edifice of complex concepts is built.

L-model-of-computation.statement: Luthier contains a model of computation that you keep testing and simplifying and must keep active, through selective forgetting or aggregation, justified by its use on a particular case.

L-modelgraph-parammanager.statement: Clean separation of the ModelGraph and ParameterManager structures.

L-models-as-well-typed-objects.statement: Biological models are well-typed objects where types are molecular states, identity paths are symmetries, and composition emerges from dependent type operations.

L-module-is-record.statement: A module is a record whose components are its definitions, so qualifying with the dot is the same as projecting.

L-monad-vs-applicative-validation.statement: A monad stops at the first failure (fit for a pipeline) while validating by hand wants the full list of violations (an applicative that accumulates errors), and the context decides between the two.

L-monads-in-luthier-question.statement: Open doubt whether monads or functors must be writable in Luthier, as Haskell has them.

L-must-be-useful.statement: Luthier must be useful and take root in something real, not stay purely theoretical, so it hits reality and reveals its limits.

L-mutation-and-ownership.statement: The core could include controlled mutation cells and linear or affine ownership for in-place mutation without garbage collection.

L-mutual-test-chain.statement: The MAP is tested with the likelihood as the likelihood is tested with the sampler, a closed chain where the algorithm produces a record and the test is a predicate over it.

L-name-real.statement: Name the real type Real rather than R.

L-name-the-patches.statement: The patches made in the work should be named as patches and noted in the plan rather than passing as specification.

L-name-the-pattern-library.statement: The verification structure the pattern builds is named Library, not Luthier the language; an instance is a program that passed its tests and can show it, so the adjective tested is superfluous.

L-nan-inf-not-reals.statement: Since Float64 is a Real, NaN and overflow to infinity are always errors, and a meaningful infinity is requested in the type via ExtendedReal.

L-native-extern-agree.statement: Each concept is written twice, native in Luthier as the slow conceptual reference and extern in Python as the fast version, and the test is that they agree; extern always, law always, native only when the law does not determine the operation.

L-need-written-objectives.statement: Without the project's objectives written down, a model deciding within its margin has nothing to measure its decisions against.

L-negative-controls.statement: A test is diagnostic only if a wrong version fails it, so negative controls (a case that must fail) are needed, since a law nothing exercises certifies nothing.

L-nested-certified-structure.statement: A structure can carry another certified structure as a named component, the laws reaching into it with a dot and quantifying over two types at once, with the precision parameter propagating through the composition.

L-new-type-from-recursion-or-laws.statement: Only recursion (infinite freedom) or laws (refinement) generate a new named type; a product or sum without laws deserves no new name.

L-newton-raphson-toy-application.statement: Writing Newton-Raphson with all its invariants typed is Luthier's first concrete application and toy model.

L-next-recursor-syntax.statement: What to attack next, in order: choose the recursor (without the dependent one there are no general paths proven by induction), then the concrete syntax.

L-no-exact-equality-floats.statement: == does not decide over floats or arrays; comparison is an approximate relation with a tolerance (tolOf n = 8 n eps, the slack declared once).

L-no-inheritance-polymorphism.statement: Luthier would not incorporate C++-style derived classes or polymorphism.

L-no-parameterless-lambda.statement: A parameterless lambda should not exist: without time or effects \ () { a + a } and a + a are the same value, a consequence of the commutativity of statements.

L-no-pdfs-doi-link.statement: No PDFs or books are committed to git; the DOI is the pointer to each source, so for sources the repository points instead of containing.

L-no-principle-without-example.statement: No principle enters the specification without an example worked by hand in the candidate notation.

L-no-project-python-scripts.statement: Luthier's intent is that Luciano write no project-dedicated Python except the functions called through extern, and he asks whether the work is making patches.

L-no-value-without-passing-check.statement: There is no way to hold a value of a subtype without its predicate having been evaluated or proved; the check runs when the value is built.

L-nonunivocal-functions.statement: The language must natively model non-univocal functions, functions with error, samples.

L-normalvec-uniform-law.statement: normalVec gets a law for the first time: its integral transform is uniform.

L-note-not-field-data.statement: A note a model wrote inside a data table is not a field datum and must not be read back as one.

L-novel-evidence-combination.statement: Luthier adds no new expressiveness over Lean or Agda; its novelty is the evidence regime that joins laws in types, sampling with named generators and statistical levels, hash-tied evidence, and results carrying which laws they rest on.

L-number-generator-limits-scale.statement: A number generator needs explicit limit values and a linear or logarithmic scale (with special values and their weight), the limits carried in the type, so a Float64 without limits in its type is a static error if the binding does not supply them.

L-number-theory-record.statement: Numeric code is written once over a theory of numbers, a record with carrier, operations and equality; Real is its ideal model and Float64, intervals, Rational are others, filled through a per-file hole as in the ML functor.

L-numeric-tests-not-logic.statement: The aim of the first version is to generate numeric tests, not to do propositional logic.

L-object-classifier-laws.statement: Luthier has a kind of object classifier: predicates about types that are the laws, the names.

L-object-has-head.statement: Every object has a head: a type whose body names its laws, so there are no free-standing laws that define.

L-object-is-record-type.statement: An object is always a record type including its carrier, defined by its laws; implementations are its values, so there is never more than one body per name and translations always work.

L-objective-from-list.statement: An Objective should not be drawn by rejection (random functions almost never match their declared gradient) but taken from an explicit list of registered values, such as the project's own objective and a quadratic.

L-objective-laws.statement: Objective carries its laws: the gradient is that of its value and the step matrix is positive semidefinite, plus the laws of any maximizer.

L-objects-are-cycles.statement: When the invariants of several definitions need each other they are a co-dependent object defined together in one simultaneous definition against a type that ties them with laws; objects are the cycles of the definition graph.

L-one-binding-form.statement: One binding form name : Type appears identically in declaration, parameter, dependent type and pair, with A -> B sugar for (_ : A) -> B and the dot disappearing.

L-one-body-per-name.statement: Giving a name both a body of laws and := extern is two bodies for one name, forbidden; the two styles that seemed to coexist are one badly written.

L-one-generator-per-type.statement: A generator written over an alias is the generator of the type the alias names, and two generators for the same type are an error.

L-one-name-per-thing.statement: Do not declare the same thing under two distinct names.

L-only-types-and-functions.statement: Luthier collapses the many constructs into a single kind: only types and functions exist, and functions are themselves a type.

L-opaque-body-is-law-conjunction.statement: The body of an opaque type is the conjunction of the laws over it and its operations (Table := NonNegative & Reflexive & IntColumn); an operation the laws do not name stays outside the cycle.

L-opaque-type.statement: A large machine value like a numpy array enters Luthier as an opaque extern type whose values pass through untouched; such values have no equality, and comparing them is a function to R with tolerance.

L-operations-by-ops-or-properties.statement: A mathematical object's operations can be defined through other operations or by their properties; when both, a theorem connects them, and the elemental set is not unique.

L-optimize-needs-strong-certificates.statement: Type, certification and measurement are one idea from three sides; optimizing over weak certificates is worse than not optimizing, so generators and certificate reach come before selection, which picks only among covering implementations and records the chosen one in each result's provenance.

L-optimize-own-rules.statement: Since he invents the language it follows his rules, so he can optimize the rules to make manipulating programs easy.

L-oracle-vs-postcondition.statement: An oracle gives an external reference to compare against, beyond an intrinsic postcondition, though abstractly both are predicates over arguments and output returning a verdict.

L-order-is-confluence.statement: Evaluation order is free for pure terms by confluence (Church-Rosser), not by purity, so the order is a strategy and a parameter, not a truth.

L-original-vs-derivative-types.statement: Some types are original (made from audios and questionnaires) and all the rest are derivative, results of functions, so they necessarily have structure.

L-own-contributions-vs-precedents.statement: Theory-with-equality, models as records and laws run as tests have precedents (Maude views, Lean structures, QuickCheck); three contributions are own (the cone-hash certificate, R10, the object as a strongly connected component).

L-parser-leniency.statement: What the parser rejects does not matter unless there are weighty theoretical reasons.

L-particle-filtering-paths.statement: The exponential explosion of the path space is handled by particle filtering: running several stochastic programs in parallel exploring different paths.

L-passthrough-or-orchestrator.statement: Luthier can be a language the code passes through or an orchestrator pointing outward, and both are fine with passage between them.

L-path-cost-estimate.statement: Each execution path carries an estimate of its characteristics: compute time above all, also error, memory, and where it runs.

L-path-equivalence-core.statement: Path equivalence, proving that different implementations are equivalent, is Luthier's fundamental and hardest concept.

L-paths-implementations.statement: One function can be implemented in many ways (paths), each with its own precision and speed, and the equivalence between implementations is seen through the paths.
